articles.title: In 2007, Serena Williams helped fund a secondary school in rural Kenya and backed a second in 2010; years after their openings, both schools are still operating as part of Kenya's public education system
articles.summary: Tennis legend Serena Williams is known for her record-breaking career on the court, but two secondary schools she helped establish in rural Kenya have
articles.body: Tennis legend Serena Williams is known for her record-breaking career on the court, but two secondary schools she helped establish in rural Kenya have left a legacy beyond sports. In 2007 and 2010, Williams partnered with Hewlett-Packard (HP) and the nonprofit Build African Schools to fund and open two schools in the East African country. More than a decade later, both institutions continue to operate as places of learning and are integrated into Kenya’s national education system, according to Build African Schools.The organisation identifies the institutions as Matooni Serena Williams Secondary School and Wee Serena Williams Secondary School. Its website says both remain open, highlighting how investments in permanent educational infrastructure can continue serving communities long after the initial projects are completed. The initiative was designed to help children in rural areas gain access to secondary education, while HP’s involvement brought computers and other technology into the classrooms.A school in rural KenyaThe first project was Matooni Serena Williams Secondary School, located in the rural Makueni region of eastern Kenya. According to a report published by Kenyan newspaper The Standard on November 15, 2008, Williams travelled to the remote village of Matooni to open the school she had helped build. Her arrival drew residents who welcomed the tennis star with songs and dances. The report described the journey from Nairobi as difficult, with damaged roads making travel through the mountainous region challenging.The school was built under the Build African Schools initiative, founded by Patrick O’Sullivan, in partnership with HP. Its initial structure had four classrooms and was expected to welcome its first students in January 2009.During the opening, Williams encouraged local residents to recognise education as a route to opportunity. The report quoted her as saying, “Education can produce a lot and open the doors for the kids.”The project was intended to give children in the surrounding area an opportunity to continue their studies after primary school. Without access to a nearby secondary institution, students in rural communities can face additional difficulties pursuing further education, including the costs and practical challenges associated with travelling longer distances. The school’s construction therefore addressed a basic but important need: providing a permanent place where students could continue learning.A second school opened in 2010Williams returned to Kenya in February 2010 to support the second project, Wee Serena Williams Secondary School, in the Makueni region. On February 23, she officially opened the institution and unveiled a computer laboratory established through HP’s involvement in the Build African Schools programme. Kenyan broadcaster Capital FM reported that students and local residents welcomed the opening.Williams, who was also serving as a global ambassador for HP, spoke about the importance of education in helping children build their futures. “This is a really special moment to build this school that’s going to help so many kids and build so many futures,” she said, according to the report.The computer laboratory was another significant component of the initiative. HP supplied computers and other technology, helping students gain exposure to digital tools that were not readily available in every rural school.A separate report published by The Standard in February 2010, described Williams teaching students how to use computers during her visit. Students expressed excitement about learning computer skills, with the report highlighting how the equipment could help bridge the digital divide between rural and urban communities.The visit also demonstrated that the initiative extended beyond constructing buildings. It brought together educational infrastructure, technology and encouragement from a prominent international sports figure.How the schools are managed todayBuild African Schools says both institutions remain open and are integrated into Kenya’s national education system. Its wider operating model involves constructing permanent school buildings and handing responsibility for their ongoing management to community boards, with support from Kenya’s Ministry of Education.The organisation’s school directory lists Matooni Serena Williams Secondary School as a 2007 project in Kitui County and Wee Serena Williams Secondary School as a 2010 project in the same county. It also says its schools are permanent structures managed by the communities they serve and integrated into the national education system.This distinction is important: Williams helped fund the projects through a partnership, while the long-term operation of the schools rests within the local educational framework. The organisation’s current website provides the clearest available confirmation that both institutions continue to operate, although the sources cited here do not provide recent enrolment figures or independent inspections of either school.Williams’ wider commitment to educationThe Kenyan schools formed part of Williams’ broader interest in expanding educational opportunities. In February 2010, news agency reports said she wanted to help build a school each year in parts of Africa where access to education remained limited.Her involvement in the two Kenyan projects also included a partnership with HP, which supported the schools with computer facilities and training. The initiative connected the tennis champion’s public profile with a practical local effort to improve educational access.For the communities served by Matooni and Wee, the significance of the projects lies not simply in the presence of Williams’ name on the schools, but in the continued availability of places where students can learn.According to Build African Schools, both institutions remain part of Kenya’s national education system today. Their continued operation offers a long-term perspective on philanthropy: while a school opening may be a single event, the classrooms it creates can serve successive generations of students.You use AI every day. articles.body: Prince Harry has personally donated £1.1 million to the BBC Children in Need charity, one of the largest individual sums publicly given by a member of the British royal family. The Duke of Sussex announced the gift on Tuesday, 9 September 2025, during a visit to Nottingham, his first to Britain in five months. Children in Need said the money would help young people in communities blighted by violence and knife crime, especially in Nottingham. Harry, 40, said knife crime continues to devastate lives and that he had been committed to this work for over a decade, adding that he could not “look away”.How will Prince Harry’s £1.1 million donation support young peopleAccording to Reuters, Children in Need said the money would help young people in communities blighted by violence and knife crime, especially in Nottingham. The charity has raised more than £1 billion since 1980 to support charities and projects across Britain.Harry, 40, told the audience that Nottingham has his respect, his commitment and a permanent place in his heart. He and his wife Meghan visited the city on their first official engagement eight years earlier.Why is Prince Harry calling for action against knife crimeHarry said that violence affecting young people, particularly knife crime, continues to devastate lives, cut futures short and leave families grieving. He said he had been committed to this work for over a decade and that the urgency was now greater than when he began. He added: "We cannot, and must not, and will not look away."Harry acknowledged that his contribution alone would not be enough to make a difference. He said the government, police, schools and businesses would all need to work together.Why has Prince Harry’s UK visit attracted media attentionRoyal charitable organisations often donate millions and individuals often give to causes, but such gifts are not publicly disclosed. It said King Charles was thanked by organisers for an unspecified donation to an appeal for survivors of the 2023 earthquake in Turkey and Syria, a cause also supported by Prince William and his wife Kate. William has also recently given unspecified sums to mental health organisations, charities helping in Ukraine and after a Caribbean hurricane, and a London food bank that suffered a burglary.Harry arrived from his home in California on Monday. He laid flowers at the grave of his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth, on the third anniversary of her death, then attended an awards ceremony for ill children. The agency added that much of the media focus had been on whether he would meet his father, King Charles, whom he had not seen for 20 months. articles.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab
articles.summary: Uganda has been helping Somalia battle an insurgency led by the al-Shabab militant group since 2007.
articles.body:
Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.

Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.

He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.

Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.

A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.

Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.

"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.

On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".

The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.

The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.

The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.

In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.

An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.

Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.

After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.

They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.

Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.

This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.

Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.

A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

articles.title: A Texas man was arrested after stealing human remains from a cemetery mausoleum and throwing a bucket of bones over an FBI office fence; his mother alerted police after he asked her for money.
articles.summary: A Texas man has been arrested after allegedly removing human remains from a cemetery mausoleum and throwing a bucket containing human bones over the fence
articles.body: A Texas man has been arrested after allegedly removing human remains from a cemetery mausoleum and throwing a bucket containing human bones over the fence of an FBI office in Dallas. The investigation into the incident began after the man's mother contacted police about his unusual request for money to hire a moving truck. Authorities later uncovered videos allegedly showing him with human remains at his home and carrying out the incident outside the federal building. The case has also brought renewed attention to his previous arrest in Dallas.Texas man arrested after human remains allegedly stolen from cemetery mausoleumMichael Chadwick Fry, 41, of Bartonville, Texas, was arrested on March 18, 2026, following an investigation involving the Bartonville Police Department, Denton Police Department and FBI agents.According to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, investigators received information suggesting that Fry had unlawfully removed human remains from a cemetery in Denton County. The investigation eventually led officers to the Independent Order of Odd Fellows (IOOF) Cemetery in Denton, where they discovered a damaged mausoleum with remains missing from inside.The Denton Police Department confirmed the discovery. The department said it had been informed on March 18 that human remains recovered during an investigation by Bartonville police might have been taken from the cemetery.Following a search of the site, officers found damage to the mausoleum and confirmed that remains were missing. Authorities also said the next of kin had been notified.The case was being investigated by Bartonville police, with Denton officers providing assistance. The involvement of the FBI added a federal dimension to an investigation that began with reports of missing remains.What led investigators to Michael Chadwick FryThe circumstances that brought Fry to the attention of authorities emerged through information provided by his family.According to the arrest warrant affidavit reported the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, Fry's mother contacted police on March 16 after he approached her asking for money to rent a U-Haul truck.When she asked why he needed the vehicle, he reportedly told her that he had a body that needed to be moved. His mother said he became angry and left her home after the conversation.Concerned by the statement, she contacted the Bartonville Police Department. Investigators subsequently circulated information to neighbouring law enforcement agencies to help locate Fry and watch for potentially suspicious activity.His sister also contacted authorities and provided information about a video she believed Fry had recorded and uploaded online.The footage reportedly showed him outside the FBI's Dallas field office with a bucket containing what he described as human remains. This information became an important part of the investigation and helped officers connect the cemetery case with the incident at the federal building.A YouTube video showed the bucket being thrown over the FBI fenceAccording to CBS News Texas, investigators reviewed a video posted on Fry's YouTube account that allegedly showed him throwing a closed white bucket over the security fence at the FBI's Dallas field office.In the footage, Fry reportedly referred to the contents as Elizabeth's remains and indicated that he wanted to attract the attention of federal agents.The arrest affidavit stated that Fry appeared to be attempting to get the FBI involved in what he considered wrongdoing by Denton County officials connected to an earlier arrest.An FBI special agent later informed investigators that the bucket contained numerous bones that appeared to be human. The remains were sent for forensic examination.Authorities also reviewed two other videos from Fry's YouTube account. These allegedly showed him holding a human skull at his residence in Bartonville. The skull reportedly had dirt, hair and other natural material still attached to it. Fry identified it as Elizabeth Virginia Lyon in the videos.According to the affidavit, an investigating officer believed the skull and the bones recovered from the FBI premises belonged to the same set of remains. However, forensic examination was needed to establish their connection.Investigators found evidence of another cemetery theftThe investigation also uncovered information about a separate incident involving human remains in Oklahoma City.According to the Bartonville Police Department's statement, investigators determined that Fry had allegedly stolen an urn containing human remains from a cemetery in Oklahoma City. Police there had already opened an investigation into the theft in February 2026.Fry's mother also provided investigators with information about searches for cemeteries recorded in the vehicle he used. The GPS records reportedly showed searches for three locations, including one cemetery in Arlington, Texas, and two in Oklahoma City.She also told authorities that she had noticed a new shovel at the property and that Fry had recently started locking a backyard shed, something she said he had not regularly done before.Separately, FBI agents found evidence at the Denton cemetery suggesting that a coffin had been removed from the mausoleum.What charges does Fry face following his arrestFollowing the investigation, Bartonville police arrested Fry at his residence in the 500 block of Oakwood Drive on March 18. According to CBS News Texas, Fry was charged with two counts of abuse of a corpse and one count of tampering with evidence, a third-degree felony under Texas law.FOX 4 reported that abuse of a corpse is a state jail felony. The charges relate to the alleged handling and removal of human remains. Court records also showed that Fry had been arrested more than two dozen times since 2003. His previous charges included assault causing bodily injury, burglary, theft, disorderly conduct, criminal mischief and resisting arrest.Fry was previously arrested after crashing into a Dallas television stationAccording to FOX 4, Fry was arrested in 2018 after repeatedly driving a rented pickup truck into the station's building while the morning news programme was being broadcast.After getting out of the vehicle, he reportedly threw sheets of paper across the pavement. He also left behind a bright orange duffel bag, prompting police to establish a security perimeter and call in a bomb squad.Investigators later determined that Fry was upset about a 2012 incident in Denton County in which sheriff's deputies fatally shot his friend during a confrontation involving a vehicle.FOX 4 reported that Fry had been a passenger in the vehicle involved in that earlier incident. Police said he was trying to attract media attention during the 2018 episode. No injuries were reported, and he was charged with criminal mischief.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: On April 10, 1912, a Titanic passenger mailed a letter to Berlin from the ship's onboard post office; he described it as a magnificent floating town and hoped to meet the recipient again the following year
articles.summary: A letter written by a Canadian businessman shortly before the Titanic began its first voyage offers a glimpse into the final days of a passenger who never
articles.body: A letter written by a Canadian businessman shortly before the Titanic began its first voyage offers a glimpse into the final days of a passenger who never returned home.George Graham, a first-class passenger travelling from Southampton, England, to New York, wrote to a business colleague in Berlin, Germany, on April 10, 1912. In the letter, he apologised for forgetting to send his greetings earlier and expressed hope that they would meet the following year again. Four days later, the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic, killing Graham and many others on board.The letter survived the disaster and was eventually sold for $16,100 at an auction conducted by Spink Smythe in New York City. According to a report published by World Record Academy on February 23, 2009, the sale established a world record for the most expensive letter from the Titanic.Graham was from Harriston, Canada, and worked as a sales manager for the Eaton's department store company. He had boarded the Titanic at Southampton with a first-class ticket numbered 112053 and was staying in cabin B-52.The letter was posted in Southampton shortly before the ship departed on April 10 for its planned transatlantic journey to New York. Although Graham did not survive the voyage, his letter remained preserved and later became an important item connected with the disaster.What George Graham wrote in his letterThe letter was addressed to a business colleague in Berlin. Graham wrote about a greeting he had forgotten to send at the beginning of April.He explained that he had reached London late on Sunday and had been occupied with work the following day. By the time he remembered the message, several days had already passed.Graham wrote, "I am sorry that I neglected to send you a wire on the first of April, but I forgot all about it until Tuesday, you see." He continued by explaining his busy schedule and asking the recipient to accept his delayed wishes.The final part of the message was particularly significant in light of what happened days later. Graham wrote, "I hope to see you next year and that you and your good wife will enjoy good health." However, the Titanic never reached its destination.How the letter survived and reached an auctionAccording to World Record Academy, the letter was mailed in Southampton before the Titanic left England. Its survival made it one of the rare pieces of correspondence associated with passengers aboard the ship.The letter also retained several original postal features. Its second page could be folded to form an envelope-like postal cover, with the White Star Line logo on the reverse. A two-and-a-half-penny stamp was attached to the address section.The auction description also recorded signs of ageing and previous display. These included uneven discolouration on parts of the letter and several pieces of plastic tape remaining along its edges.However, the tape did not affect the readability of the writing, and the letter was otherwise described as being in very good condition.Spink Smythe later sold the letter in New York for $16,100. World Record Academy reported the sale as a record for a letter associated with the Titanic.A final message that gave his wife false hopeGraham's letter was not the only message he sent before the disaster. According to the account cited by World Record Academy, he sent a telegram to his wife in Canada hours before the Titanic struck an iceberg. In that message, he said he was well and indicated that he expected to arrive in New York on Wednesday.His wife received the telegram on Tuesday morning, when reports of the Titanic disaster were already circulating. Because the message said Graham was safe, she initially believed that he had survived the sinking.Litzenberger, quoted in the report, explained that the telegram had led her to misunderstand what had happened. The hope did not last. Days later, Graham's wife was informed that his body had been recovered from the North Atlantic.The Titanic struck an iceberg during its maiden voyage and sank in April 1912.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas farmer whose family has worked the same land since 1953 now earns $200,000 a year by leasing 600 of his 2,400 acres for solar panels, helping keep the remaining farm alive after devastating crop losses
articles.summary: For generations, the Cargil family has made a living from the wide, dry farmland surrounding Uvalde in southwest Texas.
articles.body: For generations, the Cargil family has made a living from the wide, dry farmland surrounding Uvalde in southwest Texas. But farming has never offered much certainty. Weather can erase months of work in a single night, while drought, irrigation limits and rising costs can make even a successful harvest difficult to sustain. For Steve Cargil, a 67-year-old farmer whose family has worked the property since 1953, an unlikely source of stability eventually emerged from the changing energy landscape. Scroll down to read the details.A farm facing an uncertain futureAccording to a BBC report, Cargil once expected one of his three children to eventually take over the operation, just as he had inherited the responsibility from his father. That plan became less certain after a devastating hailstorm in 2018 destroyed cabbage and onion crops that Cargil and his son Ryan had spent months cultivating.The loss exposed how vulnerable the family business had become. None of Cargil's children wanted to farm full time, leaving him to consider not only the future of the property but also his own retirement. The solution came through a portion of the family's land rather than abandoning farming altogether, adds the BBC report.600 acres become an unexpected lifelineThe BBC report further explains that Cargil leased 600 acres of his 2,400-acre property to OCI Energy for a large solar installation. The report states that the arrangement now provides him with about $200,000 annually, creating a reliable income stream alongside his remaining agricultural operation.The lease has become particularly valuable during a prolonged drought. With less land requiring irrigation, Cargil can concentrate his available water resources on the acreage he continues to farm. The additional income also provides a buffer against volatile expenses, including fuel, fertilizer and other necessities, adds the online report.Why Texas farms are attracting solar developersThe September 2026 report explains that Cargil's experience reflects a much larger transformation taking place across Texas. The state has rapidly expanded its solar generation as electricity demand rises alongside population growth.Texas added 15.8% to its population between 2015 and 2025, increasing pressure on its already enormous power system. Solar has become attractive because projects can be developed relatively quickly, while falling technology costs have made large-scale installations increasingly competitive.The report also states that farmers are central to that expansion because utility-scale solar projects require broad stretches of relatively flat land. Long-term leases can provide families with predictable income for decades, sometimes helping fund retirement plans, family trusts or continued agricultural operations.The rural debate over solarThe expansion has not been universally welcomed. In parts of rural Texas, residents have raised concerns about the clearing of trees, changes to the landscape, drainage and the presence of large battery-storage facilities.In Franklin County, opponents have pushed back against solar developments and argued that rural communities should have greater influence over where projects are built. Their concerns highlight a growing tension: solar can provide farmers with substantial financial security while simultaneously transforming the countryside that surrounds them.A different future for the Cargil farmFor Cargil, however, the equation is more straightforward. The solar lease has given his family a financial cushion without requiring him to give up the agricultural land that remains central to his identity.The possibility that the farm could eventually reach another generation now seems less remote. What began as an unexpected land-use decision has become a way to keep an old family enterprise standing in an increasingly difficult farming environment.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Who was the female pilot in the Learjet 60 crash? Intense social media speculation over Alexandra Dudgeon, Nathalia Filguerias as identity kept under wraps
articles.summary: The identity of the female pilot heard communicating with air traffic controllers moments before a Learjet 60 crashed in Florida, killing all nine people
articles.body: The identity of the female pilot heard communicating with air traffic controllers moments before a Learjet 60 crashed in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, has triggered intense speculation on social media. Two names, Alexandra Dudgeon and Nathalia Filgueiras, have surfaced online, but authorities have not officially identified the aircraft's pilots or passengers. "To everyone reaching out and posting my LinkedIn profile all over social media, I was not involved in the accident. Thank you for checking in," Dudgeon apparently released a statement.The Learjet 60, registered as N722BD, crashed in a residential area of Greenacres in Palm Beach County on November 1. The aircraft had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.While the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed that nine people were aboard, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and local authorities had not released their identities as of November 2.The speculation intensified after recordings of the final communications between the aircraft and air traffic control circulated online. A female voice can be heard reporting icing conditions and moderate turbulence before the situation deteriorates rapidly and the crew declares an emergency.Who is Alexandra Dudgeon?Alexandra Dudgeon's name began circulating after social media users linked her to Upper Jets, an aviation company, and identified her as a Learjet 60 pilot and second-in-command (SIC). A professional profile attributed to Dudgeon reportedly lists her as an LR-60 Pilot SIC. Users also pointed to an image on her LinkedIn profile that they said showed an aircraft bearing the same registration number as the Learjet involved in the crash, N722BD.Why is Nathalia Filgueiras's name circulating?Another name being discussed online is Nathalia Filgueiras, a Florida pilot who attracted attention in 2023 after earning her private pilot's licence while still in high school.According to a CBS12 report published on October 24, 2023, Filgueiras was then a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton High School in Palm Beach County. She obtained her private pilot's licence in September that year, before getting her driver's licence.She had started ground school in 2020 and accumulated 88 hours of flight time, according to the report. Her father, who had started flying recreationally in 2018, also helped her learn about aviation.The School District of Palm Beach County funded her private pilot's licence through its Aviation Academy.At the time, Filgueiras said she hoped to become a commercial airline pilot or fly private jets.Her name resurfaced following the Learjet crash, with social media users claiming she was the female pilot aboard the aircraft. Some posts have cited alleged social media activity and a purported connection to the Learjet 60.What happened in the final moments before the Learjet crash?The Learjet 60 was flying from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas when the crew reported encountering icing conditions, moderate turbulence and precipitation.According to flight-tracking data and air traffic control recordings reviewed by Flightradar24, the crew requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet in search of better flying conditions.Shortly after receiving clearance, the aircraft began losing altitude rapidly. The pilot reported an accelerating descent, with the rate eventually reaching 20,000 feet per minute, alongside an overspeed condition.The final communications included a warning: "We're going to crash into the ground."The aircraft descended more than 32,000 feet per minute at one point, according to Flightradar24's tracking data, before crashing near Military Trail in Palm Beach County.All nine people aboard died. The FAA and NTSB are investigating the crash, and the cause has not yet been established.While the female voice in the cockpit recordings has fuelled questions about the identity of the pilot, neither Alexandra Dudgeon nor Nathalia Filgueiras has been officially identified as an occupant of the aircraft. The identities of all nine people remain unconfirmed publicly.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

Together they would support the reforestation of Mutuba trees in Uganda for three years. The initiative described the work as focused equally on people, animals and the environment.The same post said this approach was needed to counter the effects of deforestation in Africa. It listed climate change, species extinction, polluted groundwater and the loss of economic livelihoods as problems the work would tackle. It added that the Jane Goodall Institute had been involved in Uganda for many years. In its words, the staff's networks and their understanding of local needs and of regional animal and plant life were "indispensable prerequisites" for success.Why are fig fruits important for Uganda's chimpanzeesAccording to the 2020 post, reforesting tropical forests would restore the habitat of chimpanzees living in Uganda. It also said the effort contributes to environmental preservation and fosters sustainable development.How do Mutuba trees create sustainable jobs in UgandaThe 2020 post said the Mutuba tree helps to create sustainable jobs because its bark can be harvested regularly and processed into barkcloth. The 2023 post said the bark has a history dating back to ancient times in Southern Uganda and can be made into barkcloth without causing harm.According to the 2023 post, rampant deforestation in recent decades threatened both the Mutuba tree and the tradition of barkcloth processing. It set out to showcase the cultural, economic and ecological advantages of the Mutuba fig tree while preserving the craft.What was the 'Wrapping Nature in Culture' initiativeAccording to the 2023 post, a total of 15,000 Mutuba tree cuttings were distributed between November 2020 and November 2023. articles.title: No successful infiltration across LoC in 2026 as J&K sees sharp decline in terror violence
articles.summary: Terror related violence in Jammu & Kashmir has fallen to its lowest level in decades suggesting a strong hint of return to normalcy, sources in the Army
articles.body: Terror related violence in Jammu & Kashmir has fallen to its lowest level in decades suggesting a strong hint of return to normalcy, sources in the Army said.According to Army sources and data available on the South Asia Terrorism Portal (SATP), terror-related fatalities in the Union Territory are at an all-time low since the portal began recording data in 2000.The decline is part of a broader trend over the years, with the drop in violence particularly pronounced in 2026.As many as 23 terrorists have been killed in Jammu and Kashmir so far this year, according to SATP data available till October 31. Fatalities among security personnel have, for the first time since 2000, fallen to single digits, with just two deaths reported during the period. Of the 23 terrorists killed, the vast majority were of Pakistani origin, an Army source said.The years 2025 and 2026, till October 31, are the only two years since 2000 in which total terror-related fatalities across all categories have remained in double digits. While 2025 recorded 92 fatalities, including those killed in the Pahalgam terror attack, the figure for the first ten months of 2026 stands at 28.The highest number of fatalities in Jammu and Kashmir since 2000 was recorded in 2001, when 4,011 people were killed, including 1,024 civilians, 628 security personnel and 2,345 terrorists. Another 14 fatalities were classified as unspecified, according to SATP.The portal also records just two civilian deaths in terror-related violence this year. Fatalities among security personnel had remained in double digits every year since 2000, while civilian fatalities had also remained in double digits over the same period.Traditionally, most terror-related violence in Jammu and Kashmir takes place during the warmer months, with incidents declining in winter. According to sources in the security establishment, around 120–140 terrorists are currently believed to be present in the Union Territory.An Army source said there has not been a single successful infiltration attempt along the Line of Control (LoC) so far this year. Infiltration attempts generally decline during winter as many mountain passes and the higher reaches of the Pir Panjal range, which flanks the Kashmir Valley from the southwest, become snowbound.Another significant development is the reported absence of local recruitment into terrorist ranks in Jammu and Kashmir this year, continuing a declining trend.According to available information, 146 locals joined terrorist groups in 2021. The number fell to 121 in 2022, 19 in 2023 and four in 2024. Just one local joined terrorist ranks in 2025, while no fresh recruitment has been reported so far in 2026, according to security sources.The law-and-order situation in the Union territory has also improved, with no bandh calls or incidents of stone-pelting reported so far this year, according to security sources. No such incidents were reported in 2025 either, they said.In comparison, Manipur has recorded 100 fatalities in violence-related incidents so far this year, including 73 civilians, three security personnel and 24 insurgents, according to SATP data.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants
articles.summary: At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness, our political editor writes.
articles.body:
At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago – and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.

"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.

The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.

Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.

But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend .

It is worth examining this policy throughout the last year or so, as it is instructive in how we have arrived at today's announcement.

Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants

Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists

In November last year, Mahmood set out a plan called "a fairer pathway to settlement".

The idea was opinions on her instincts would be sought in a consultation. And boy, were there plenty of opinions offered.

Around 200,000 people contributed to the consultation, of which 140,000 responses came from visa holders themselves I'm told.

"It's been a colossal exercise and a genuine one," is how one Whitehall source put it to me, claiming: "We have taken the time to get this right."

Or is the real truth that they have buckled under political pressure from their own side – and a change of prime minister?

Mahmood said last year that she felt compelled to act because "between 2021 and 2024, we have seen net migration of an additional 2.6 million people. Around one in every 30 people in this country today arrived in these four years." It is what critics have labelled "the Boriswave", named for the changes made under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson.

And, Mahmood argued, it was important to act with urgency, as very soon significant numbers of those recent arrivals would start qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, or ILR.

"Migrants on lower wages who bring non-working dependants and children are likely to present significant fiscal costs to the UK.

"It is therefore right that we apply more stringent controls for this group before they qualify for settled status," she said, adding: "Under our current rules, they will usually qualify for benefits payments and council housing five years after arrival.

"As the majority of this group began arriving from 2022 onwards, this is currently set to begin in 2027. We consult here on a separate baseline qualifying period, of 15 years, for this group."

But plenty within the Labour Party and beyond were uncomfortable – and yes, they cited fairness, or the perceived lack of it, in mounting their criticisms.

As the now Housing Secretary Angela Rayner put it in March , before she returned to government, the ideas were "un-British" because they involved "moving the goalposts" - migrants who had arrived in good faith under one set of rules would have their future in the UK determined by the new ones.

Just a few weeks before Rayner's intervention, Mahmood had doubled down on her plans. Addressing the centre left IPPR think tank, she said "in just four years, this country experienced levels of migration it had previously seen across four decades.

"It was not just the scale, but also the nature of that change that was so destabilising."

There was more, and with a big number attached.

"We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time.

"We estimate, based on findings from the Migration Advisory Committee, that the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn. That figure would be paid for by working people in this country."

She added: "It is an affront to the idea of fairness within our migration system."

Incidentally, the £10bn figure is contested by some – or at least placed in a wider context.

The aforementioned IPPR argue that the original plans were "never in reality going to create a £10bn long-term saving, given they were meant to delay care workers' eligibility for ILR rather than prevent them from settling altogether.

"Delaying ILR would save money on welfare, whereas the £10bn figure includes much broader long run costs once care workers enter retirement, claim the state pension, and make greater use of health and social care."

Nonetheless, Mahmood's message in March left senior Conservatives privately agreeing with her – and struck by her willingness to be unflinching in her approach to the subject.

By the time I found myself in the dusty car park of a sports club near Wigan in May, waiting to talk to an ambitious by-election candidate by the name of Andy Burnham, it was clear changes were highly likely.

He told me it was important to "work hard to get the balance right" but that the "broad thrust" of what the home secretary was doing "is right".

"Broad thrust" will be the words that account for the gap between what Mahmood used to say and what she is saying today.

The Conservatives and others will seize upon the change. The Tories will argue it amounts to an "excruciating U-turn" as one senior figure described it to me, claiming it would be "deeply personally embarrassing" for the home secretary.

They also ponder how the government will choose to make the changes, as they believe if primary legislation isn't used to do it – such as via an amendment to the Immigration and Asylum Bill currently before parliament – the plans could be successfully challenged in court.

Mahmood will argue she has tried to finally arrive at a policy the widest range of people may see as fair.

We will see and hear the range of reaction she provokes in the coming hours and days.

articles.title: Isles of Scilly group collects two tonnes of marine litter
articles.summary: The group recycles netting, plastic and other rubbish picked up on the coastline.
articles.body:
More than two tonnes of litter has been picked up from the Isles of Scilly coastline in the past 18 months, according to a community group.

Scilly Coastal Clean-up, which has been sorting marine debris since February 2025, said the haul included 8,000 plastic bottles and 16,000 pieces of rope and netting.

Director Nikki Banfield said: "Scilly is at the mercy of the wind and the tides. Each rise and fall means fresh debris is deposited around our coastlines.

"The majority, around 98%, comes from far beyond our islands and can be traced to the mainland UK, Europe, Africa, America , Canada and further afield as a result of global shipping."

Banfield said the team had picked up more than 43,000 individual pieces of waste, from small pieces of plastic known as nurdles, toilet seats, wheelie bins and fridge freezers over the past 18 months.

More than one tonne of rubbish has been exported for recycling.

They have joined up with Odyssey Innovation, which recycles marine waste, and Exeter City Council to give 1.2 tonnes of rigid plastics, rope and net a new lease of life.

Banfield said a further 770kg of rope and net had also been recycled and the Council of the Isles of Scilly had disposed of 640kg of hazardous and non-recyclable waste.

Exeter City Council's recovery manager Matt Hulland said: "Plastic pollution doesn't limit itself to our peninsula beaches and waters and efforts like this highlight what an issue discarded or lost fishing gear and other plastics can be to Scilly, its people, businesses and wildlife."

articles.title: Iran calls US biggest threat to NPT, warns of stronger defence push
articles.summary: Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has called the United States the \"greatest threat\" to the global nuclear non-proliferation regime,
articles.body: Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has called the United States the "greatest threat" to the global nuclear non-proliferation regime, accusing Washington of undermining the very treaty it claims to defend.According to news agency ANI, Baghaei made the remarks during a press briefing on Monday, responding to threats by the United States targeting Iran's remaining nuclear facilities. He argued that threatening military action against a country could undermine the principles of nuclear non-proliferation and encourage states to reconsider their security policies."The United States is actually the greatest threat to the nuclear non-proliferation regime," Baghaei said. "The very expression of a threat against a country and the implicit threat that we may use a certain weapon is itself an encouragement to violate the Non-Proliferation Treaty."He further criticised the silence of international institutions, including the United Nations, the UN Security Council and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), over what he described as Washington's hostile rhetoric against Tehran."The threats being raised against us will surely make us more determined to strengthen our capabilities in our own defence," Baghaei said, warning that American threats could set a dangerous international precedent.Addressing questions about whether Tehran could reconsider its nuclear doctrine in response to military threats, Baghaei acknowledged that discussions on the issue were taking place within Iranian society and among sections of its political establishment. He linked the debate to years of American pressure and targeted assassinations of individuals associated with Iran's nuclear programme."Iran's nuclear program has been and remains absolutely peaceful, and this has been proven many times," he said.Baghaei also confirmed that Iran had no immediate plans to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), maintaining that Tehran continued to recognise its obligations under the international agreement."At the decision-making level, we are still a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and as long as Iran is a member of this treaty, it considers itself bound and obliged to comply with the obligations contained in that document," he said.The NPT, which entered into force in 1970, seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and advance nuclear disarmament. articles.title: A Louisiana man died without a will in 1956, and a 1996 court order named his daughter as heir to half a property; 30 years later, the state Supreme Court blocked a rival family's attempt to undo that inheritance ruling
articles.summary: A property dispute involving a Louisiana man who died without leaving a will in 1956 has reached the state's Supreme Court, nearly 30 years after a court
articles.body: A property dispute involving a Louisiana man who died without leaving a will in 1956 has reached the state's Supreme Court, nearly 30 years after a court recognised his daughter as the heir to his estate. In a ruling delivered on October 30, the Louisiana Supreme Court blocked an attempt by another family to overturn the 1996 inheritance decision. The judges ruled that the challenge had been brought too late under state law, leaving the earlier decision recognising Earnestine Walker's inheritance rights intact.According to the judgement, the dispute concerned a piece of land in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, where two families claimed ownership through different records dating back several decades. At the centre of the disagreement was Augustine Howard's 50% share of the property, known in court documents as Tract 2.The case began as a disagreement over who owned the land but eventually turned into a legal challenge to a court order issued in 1996. That order had recognised Walker as Howard's sole heir. The opposing family argued that she should not have inherited the property under the law that existed when her father died.The Supreme Court did not decide the dispute by reconsidering Walker's eligibility under the old inheritance law, but it examined whether the rival claimants were legally allowed to challenge the 1996 decision after so many years. Its ruling overturned decisions by two lower courts and sent the case back for further proceedings.How the property dispute beganThe property's ownership history goes back to 1924, when Tract 2 was divided between Augustine Howard and Inez Howard. Each received a 50% ownership interest.Howard died in 1956 without a will. Four decades later, a court issued a judgment recognising Earnestine Walker as the sole heir to his estate. Windward Land, LLC and Michael Morris Gulley later claimed an interest in the property through Walker's ownership rights.However, another group, identified in the judgment as the Frazier-Edwards respondents, claimed ownership through Addie Edwards. Their claim was connected to a 1955 deed executed by Zephyr Johnson, who was Inez Howard's daughter and Augustine Howard's niece.The competing claims became part of a lawsuit filed by Windward Land and Gulley seeking to divide the property among its owners.During those proceedings, the Frazier-Edwards family challenged the 1996 inheritance order. They argued that Walker, described in the court documents as a child born outside marriage, could not legally have inherited Howard's estate under the law applicable in 1956.Why rival family challenged inheritanceThe family's argument relied on an earlier Louisiana inheritance law that treated children born outside marriage differently from those born within marriage.Under the law in force between 1908 and 1981, a child born outside marriage could not inherit from a parent who died without a will if that parent had children legally recognised as born within marriage.Although the provision was later declared unconstitutional, the court ruling striking it down was made retroactive only to January 1, 1975. Howard had died in 1956.The Frazier-Edwards respondents therefore argued that Walker should never have been recognised as his heir.The trial court accepted their argument and declared the 1996 inheritance judgment ineffective. It instead recognised Zephyr Johnson as Howard's rightful heir, leading to a ruling that the Frazier-Edwards respondents owned the entire property.Windward challenged that decision, arguing that the family had waited far beyond the legally permitted period to question the inheritance order.The trial court rejected Windward's request for a new trial, and an appeals court subsequently upheld the earlier decision. Windward then approached the Louisiana Supreme Court.Why Supreme Court rejected the challengeThe Supreme Court examined Louisiana Revised Statute 9:5630, which generally provides a two-year deadline for certain inheritance-related claims involving property acquired from a person recognised as an heir.The disagreement concerned who was covered by that deadline. The Frazier-Edwards respondents argued that the restriction applied only to heirs or beneficiaries directly claiming inheritance rights from the deceased person. They maintained that their claim, based on property transferred through Addie Edwards, was different. The Supreme Court disagreed.Justice Griffin, writing for the court, explained that the term "successor" was not limited to someone directly inheriting property. It could also include buyers, people receiving property as gifts and others who obtained ownership rights through transfers.The judges concluded that the Frazier-Edwards respondents were also covered by the two-year deadline. Their attempt to invalidate the 1996 judgment was therefore legally barred.The court also warned that allowing people to avoid the deadline simply by transferring property to someone else would undermine the purpose of the law, which is to provide certainty over ownership.The Supreme Court thus ruled that the 1996 inheritance judgment remained valid and had transferred Augustine Howard's 50% interest in Tract 2 to Earnestine Walker. It overturned the lower courts' decisions and returned the case to the trial court for further proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Despicable betrayal’: Top Democrat slams Haley Stevens for backing Republican candidate over El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: A Democratic congresswoman in Michigan has endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her party's nominee Abdul El-Sayed, triggering a
articles.body: A Democratic congresswoman in Michigan has endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her party's nominee Abdul El-Sayed, triggering a political storm within the party just before the US midterm elections.Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary in August, announced her support for Rogers on Sunday after appearing alongside him at a church service in Detroit. Her endorsement came amid a rising bitter public feud with El-Sayed, who had reportedly asked her to stay away from a planned joint campaign appearance."Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing her decision. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."The move drew sharp criticism from Democratic leaders, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling it a "despicable betrayal". Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel accused Stevens of abandoning the values she claimed to support.El-Sayed, however, sought to play down the development, telling reporters that he was focused on issues affecting voters, including the rising cost of living."At the end of the day I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding that "none of this matters".What led to Stevens' break with El-Sayed?The rift between the two Democrats has deepened since the August primary, reflecting wider divisions within the party over its political direction and US support for Israel.Stevens, a centrist Democrat and strong supporter of Israel, had called on El-Sayed to condemn an advertisement by an independent left-wing group linking US support for Israel to high grocery prices. El-Sayed criticised the advertisement and said it was not produced by his campaign.In a statement on Friday, Stevens said El-Sayed should stop blaming Israel for economic problems facing Michigan residents."Abdul promises to get money out of politics," she wrote. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."El-Sayed responded by accusing Stevens of trying to reopen a primary contest that had ended months earlier. He also said he did not agree with the advertisement.The two were originally expected to appear together at a church event on Sunday alongside other Democratic leaders in an effort to demonstrate party unity before Election Day. However, the planned joint appearance was called off, with Stevens instead attending a service with Rogers.Democrats react as Trump praises endorsementStevens' decision also triggered turmoil within her own office. Her longtime chief of staff resigned following the announcement, while other staff members were expected to leave, according to a person familiar with the developments."We are shocked and heartbroken," an aide said in a statement.Hertel said the endorsement showed that Stevens had "abandoned everything she claims to care about", while Schumer publicly condemned her decision to support the Republican candidate.President Donald Trump, meanwhile, praised Stevens, describing her move as an act of bravery and highlighting her support among Black and Jewish voters in Michigan.Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa, House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he had spoken to Stevens after the endorsement and encouraged her to keep speaking out.Rogers welcomed the congresswoman's backing, saying he was honoured by her support.Why the Michigan Senate race mattersThe contest between El-Sayed and Rogers is among the closely watched Senate races in Tuesday's midterm elections. The seat is currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, and Republicans have not won it since 1994.Michigan is a key battleground state, having backed Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election before voting for Trump in 2024.For Democrats, holding the seat is crucial to their efforts to regain control of the Senate. The party needs a net gain of four seats to secure a majority, making Michigan one of the most consequential contests in the election.Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County during the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters. The primary was marked by bitter exchanges and heavy outside spending, including support for Stevens from a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.Early voting in Michigan began on October 24, with more than 1.8 million people having cast ballots by Friday.You use AI every day. articles.title: Karl Bushby ends 28-year journey at mother's house in Hull
articles.summary: Crowds gathered in Hull city centre to welcome him, before he walked home to to his mother.
articles.body:
British adventurer Karl Bushby has completed his 31,000-mile (50,000 km) journey from South America to Hull in the UK, reuniting with his mother at the family home 28 years after setting off.

In November 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to complete an unbroken path back home, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until the end of the journey, and not to use transport to advance.

Earlier, crowds gathered in Hull's city centre to welcome Bushby, before he set off to complete the final few miles home to his mother Angela Bushby.

Reaching the front door, he said: “It’s good to be home. It feels surreal.“

Bushby's journey took him to four continents, with key moments including navigating through the dense jungles of the Darién Gap , crossing the frozen Bering Strait and, more recently, swimming the English Channel .

As they had agreed years earlier, Bushby's mother, Angela, waited for him at her home in Sutton Park, where she raised him.

He said: “It feels surreal. It’s the end of a 28-year journey.”

His mother, who had not seen him for a decade, told Bushby: “Where have you been?”

She told the BBC: “It’s good to have him home.

As he approached the house, he said: “This is familiar.”

But he admitted he never expected such a homecoming.

Addressing the crowd in the city centre, Bushby, when he was received by the lord mayor, Maria Coward, said: “There has never been a welcome home like this, I am sure. It's madness. An enormous thank you."

He added: "The biggest team - Earth - got me back here.”

On Sunday, when he crossed the Humber Bridge into East Yorkshire, he was met by his 36-year-old son Adam, his 12-year-old granddaughter whom he had never met, his father and brothers.

“It was amazing,” Bushby said of the reunion.

After returning to the UK, Bushby said he expected to struggle in the coming days and weeks as he readjusted to normal life.

"Everything that I am and everything that I know of me is going to go away," he said. "And that's going to be a problem. You're going to have the old identity crisis, because Karl is this [an adventurer] and has been for half his life.

"I think the old adage goes... the only thing worse than a man who can't fulfil his dreams is a man who's fulfilled his dreams... because then what?"

Bushby previously said he had always had a "wanderlust", and his opportunity to embark on this journey came following the end of his marriage, with his wife returning to Northern Ireland with their son.

Bushby said only about 15 of the 28 years were spent walking, with struggles obtaining visas, the 2007 global economic crash and Covid blamed for delays.

He often retreated to Mexico, where costs are low, between stints.

Under the rules he set for his journey, Bushby could not return to the UK to meet his family.

On rare occasions, he met his son and parents, who are divorced, in other countries.

Bushby said he set off as "penniless backpacker", often relying on handouts, or occasionally being forced to eat food discarded on roadsides.

He later secured sponsors and a book deal.

Nearing the end of the journey, he signed a deal with acclaimed German filmmaker Werner Herzog, with the pair pictured together on Shakespeare Beach, near Dover, moments after the adventurer waded ashore in October.

articles.title: Cyclone Murasu to make landfall near at Andhra coast tonight; 120 kmph winds expected
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cyclone Murasu, which has intensified into a Severe Cyclonic Storm, is expected to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cyclone Murasu, which has intensified into a Severe Cyclonic Storm, is expected to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur in the early hours of Tuesday, bringing winds of up to 120 kmph, extremely heavy rainfall and the threat of coastal flooding. The cyclone is forecast to make landfall south of Ongole between 11:30 pm on Monday and 4 am on Tuesday.According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Murasu intensified into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over the west-central and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal in the early hours of Monday. In its Press Release issued on November 2, IMD said Cyclone Murasu was centred at 14.1°N latitude and 81.4°E longitude at 8:30 am on Monday, around 160 km east-southeast of Nellore and 180 km northeast of Chennai.The IMD has warned of strong winds and heavy rainfall across several districts of Andhra Pradesh, including Krishna, Bapatla, Prakasam, Nellore, Guntur, Eluru, NTR, Palnadu and West Godavari.Chennai, Thiruvallur, Ranipet, Kancheepuram and Chengalpattu in north Tamil Nadu, along with parts of Puducherry, are also expected to experience strong winds and rainfall. Southern Odisha districts, including Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri, are also under warning. Telangana and Rayalaseema are likely to receive heavy to extremely heavy rainfall.Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has reviewed cyclone preparedness and directed officials to coordinate rescue and relief operations. Six NDRF and seven SDRF teams have been deployed, while control rooms and evacuation arrangements have been put in place.The IMD has advised a complete suspension of fishing operations along the affected coastal areas. Fishermen have been warned against venturing into the west-central Bay of Bengal until the afternoon of November 4 and along the Andhra Pradesh coast during the same period. The weather agency has also cautioned against the movement of motorboats and small ships due to dangerous sea conditions.Murasu is expected to weaken into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday morning, with wind speeds reducing to 70–80 kmph, gusting to 90 kmph.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia exits European anti-torture treaty, ends independent prison inspections
articles.summary: Russia has formally withdrawn from the council of Europe’s Convention for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment,
articles.body: Russia has formally withdrawn from the council of Europe’s Convention for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, bringing an end to the European body’s mandate to independently monitor conditions in Russian prisons, police stations and other places of detention.The withdrawal took effect on November 1, a year after Moscow notified the Council of Europe of its decision to denounce the convention on October 30, 2025. Russia had been party to the treaty since 1998.“The withdrawal of the Russian Federation marks the end of the CPT’s monitoring mandate in the country. It also marks the end of any independent monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty inside the Russian Federation,” Alan Mitchell, president of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), said in a statement.The committee said it had received numerous accounts of alleged torture and ill-treatment by Russian officials since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The allegations concerned detention facilities both in occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia.However, the CPT said it had been unable to visit Russia to examine the allegations because of the Russian authorities’ lack of cooperation. It contrasted this with Ukraine, which continues to allow the committee access to any place of detention on its territory and supports the automatic publication of its reports.Russia blocked publication of most inspection reportsDuring its membership, the CPT carried out 30 visits to Russia between 1998 and 2021, inspecting more than 450 places of detention. But Russia was the only party to the convention with a stated policy of refusing to authorise the publication of the committee’s visit reports and government responses.Only four reports were approved for publication. The unpublished findings include those from periodic and ad hoc visits, among them 10 inspections in Chechnya and the North Caucasus between 2000 and 2017. Russia can still authorise their publication.The CPT’s monitoring covers prisons, police stations, immigration detention centres, juvenile detention facilities, psychiatric hospitals and social care homes. Its delegations have the right to enter places of detention without restriction, interview detainees in private and communicate with anyone who may provide relevant information.The committee sends governments confidential reports setting out its findings and recommendations after each visit. The system is intended to prevent torture and ill-treatment through independent inspections and dialogue with national authorities, rather than to investigate or prosecute individual cases.Mitchell said independent monitoring remained a fundamental safeguard against abuse of people deprived of their liberty.The CPT will continue its work across the Council of Europe’s 46 member states. Russia left the Council of Europe in 2022, after the organisation moved to expel it following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Co-pilot of doomed Learjet flight that crashed in Florida identified as Nathalia Gadelha. She got her private pilot's license when she was 17
articles.summary: Nathalia Gadelha, a 20-year-old aspiring commercial pilot, has been identified as the co-pilot aboard the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on Sunday,
articles.body: Nathalia Gadelha, a 20-year-old aspiring commercial pilot, has been identified as the co-pilot aboard the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board. Gadelha was identified by her mother and stepfather, according to the New York Post. The aircraft crashed in Palm Beach County on November 1 while travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas.The young pilot had earned her private pilot's licence at just 17, while still attending West Boca Raton High School in Florida. She obtained the licence before getting her driver's licence and had spoken publicly about her ambition to pursue a career in commercial aviation.Gadelha began taking flying lessons in 2020 and learned from her father, who had also taken up flying as a recreational activity. By the time she obtained her licence in September 2023, she had logged 88 hours of flight time.Her training was supported by the Palm Beach County School District's Aviation Academy, which funded her private pilot's licence. She subsequently graduated from American Flyers flight school while continuing to pursue her aviation career.Who was Nathalia Gadelha?Gadelha first attracted attention in October 2023, when CBS12 News interviewed her about becoming a licensed pilot while still in high school.At the time, she was a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton High School. She had begun ground school in 2020 and completed her private pilot training through the school district's Aviation Academy.In the interview, she spoke about the unusual experience of being able to fly an aircraft before she could drive a car.Gadelha had also shared photographs of herself in aircraft cockpits on social media. One of her posts reportedly featured a Learjet 60, the same type of aircraft involved in Sunday's fatal crash.A recent social media post also described her and her boyfriend as young pilots who had obtained multiple aviation qualifications before turning 21.What happened in the Learjet 60 crash?The Learjet 60 was travelling from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas when it crashed in Palm Beach County on November 1.The aircraft went into a steep descent before hitting the ground and catching fire. All nine people aboard were killed.Air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments captured the crew reporting icing conditions, precipitation and turbulence. The pilots also requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet in an apparent attempt to find better flying conditions.Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft losing altitude at an alarming rate, with its descent eventually exceeding 20,000 feet per minute.The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board are investigating the crash. The cause has not yet been established.As the names of the pilots or the passengers were not revealed immediately after the crash, there were intense social media speculations. There were speculations about Alexandra Dudgeon and Nathalia Filgueiras, but the name that has officially been confirmed is Nathalia Gadelha. Her full name in some documents has been recorded as Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two sisters, a bag of tools and a mission to mend Bengaluru’s umbrellas
articles.summary: Two sisters in Bengaluru keep umbrella repair alive, traveling by bus with tools to mend broken umbrellas and serve customers seeking savings or sentiment.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Every morning at 7, sisters Selvi and Amaravathi set out from their Jayanagar home, boarding a bus with a bag full of umbrella repair tools. They travel through the streets of east Bengaluru, mending broken umbrellas and keeping an age-old craft alive in a world increasingly driven by overconsumption and throwaway culture.Selvi, 52, and Amaravathi, 60, moved to Bengaluru from Tamil Nadu with their parents nearly 40 years ago. “My entire family repaired umbrellas — my parents, brother and about 20 others. My sister and I would follow them through the streets, watching and learning the craft. Decades later, we are the only ones left carrying on the trade,” Selvi said.Her son, too, chose a different path, moving to Kuwait for work rather than learning the trade.The sisters travel by BMTC bus to areas such as Shivajinagar, Koramangala and Ulsoor, walking the streets with a pre-recorded audio message advertising their services. They carry spare parts, including pipes and handles, balanced carefully on their heads.Are there still enough customers in a city like Bengaluru who want their umbrellas repaired? “Plenty,” says Selvi, adding: “People who buy umbrellas for Rs 100-200 tend to discard them when they break. But someone who has spent Rs 500 on a good folding umbrella is less likely to throw it away. Some umbrellas also have sentimental value. Just the other day, a woman brought six or seven umbrellas gifted to her by her late mother and grandmother. She wanted to preserve them as family memories.”The sisters repair handles, pipes and ribs, replace fabric, and fix patches and caps. Depending on business, they earn between Rs 500-600 and Rs 1,000-1,500 a day. Daily expenses amount to around Rs 200-300, while every two months they set aside Rs 10,000 to buy spare parts from KR Market.“About 25 years ago, we worked longer hours, from 6am to 9pm, but earned less. Expenses were also lower, around Rs 25-30 a day. Now, we work until 1 or 2pm and earn more, but our expenses have risen too,” Selvi says.For Selvi and Amaravathi, however, the trade is about more than money. “I educated my children with what I earned from this work. Today, I don’t want to sit at home doing nothing. We want to honour the profession that gave us our livelihood. That is why we continue to walk the streets,” Selvi says.Will the trade survive after them? Selvi is doubtful. “I don’t think it will. This is not a skill you can simply teach someone. articles.title: CM meets Gadkari seeks early clearance of 4 highway projects
articles.summary: Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary urges Nitin Gadkari to seek early CCEA clearance for four highway projects worth Rs49,751 crore, spanning 330 km.
articles.body: Patna: Chief minister Samrat Choudhary on Monday urged Union road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari to seek early clearance from Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) for four major highway and expressway projects in Bihar, involving Rs49,751 crore. CCEA, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is set to consider the proposals after their approval by the Union govt’s Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee.Choudhary made the request during a high-level meeting with Gadkari in New Delhi. He said the four projects, together covering about 330 km, were vital for reducing logistics costs and easing traffic movement in the state. He asked the ministry to ensure final CCEA approval at the earliest, saying the corridors would give Bihar’s connectivity a new direction.The projects include NH-727AA, a two-lane bridge over Gandak river, along with a bridge and approach road connecting Manuapul in Bettiah, Bihar, with Tiwaripatti in Sevarahi, Uttar Pradesh, whose estimated cost would be Rs1,976.77 crore. The second project involves six-lane elevated and service roads on the Saristabad-Didarganj and Anisabad-Didarganj sections at Rs8,455.86 crore under the Hybrid Annuity Mode (HAM). Patna-Purnia four-lane greenfield expressway, NH-09, also under HAM, is estimated at Rs31,987.11 crore. Varanasi-Ranchi-Kolkata six-lane greenfield highway from Konki village to Lerua village is pegged at Rs7,331.40 crore under HAM.Choudhary also requested early notification of the Bihar section of Gorakhpur-Siliguri Expressway as a National Expressway. He said the state govt was fully assisting National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) in pre-construction work, while land acquisition under the 3A notification was at an advanced stage in the districts concerned. Construction of the expressway, he said, would create new bridges over north Bihar rivers and bring wide changes to the transport network.The CM discussed Raxaul-Haldia Expressway, saying land acquisition had begun after approval of its revised alignment. He described the corridor as strategically important for boosting trade with Nepal and giving Bihar direct connectivity to Haldia port, and sought early notification and approval.He further urged faster four-laning of the Muzaffarpur-Barauni section of NH-122, for which NHAI has prepared the DPR.Choudhary said 2,329 km of National Highways in Bihar had been handed to road construction department for maintenance and development. The department has sent DPRs to the Centre for six NH projects covering 323 km and costing Rs13,015 crore, including the Vikramshila bridge approach road and Mashrakh-Chakia-Bhitthamod four-lane widening.He sought early technical and financial approval for these proposals and thanked PM and Gadkari for supporting Bihar’s road infrastructure and their continued cooperation in developing the state’s wider road infrastructure network.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news.
